variant.stem_override: A 65-year-old man with seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years (currently on methotrexate + adalimumab) presents to clinic with 4 weeks of new posterior neck pain, occipital headaches, and bilateral hand and forearm paresthesias. He also reports a sense of unsteadiness and one episode of bilateral leg weakness when he briefly lost balance descending stairs. Vital signs are stable. Neurologic exam shows mild bilateral upper-extremity hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffmann sign on the right, and mild lower-extremity hyperreflexia with bilateral upgoing toes (positive Babinski) — features of an UPPER MOTOR NEURON syndrome consistent with cervical myelopathy. Cervical spine X-rays in flexion and extension show an atlantodental interval (ADI) of 5 mm in flexion (normal <3 mm; severe ≥9 mm), consistent with anterior atlantoaxial subluxation. Cervical MRI confirms pannus around the odontoid process and mild cord compression at C1–C2 with cord T2 hyperintensity at the level of compression. There is no fracture and no vertebral artery involvement on MRA.
variant.rationale_for_variant: Only the patient's sex was changed from female to male, with pronouns updated accordingly; all clinical findings, laboratory values, imaging results, and the narrative sequence remain identical. Atlantoaxial subluxation with symptomatic cervical myelopathy in long-standing seropositive erosive RA requires urgent neurosurgical evaluation regardless of the patient's sex, so the correct answer (A) is unchanged. Although RA is more prevalent in women, it occurs in men and produces the same cervical-spine complications managed by the same guidelines. This variant probes whether clinicians or models might underweight the severity of RA-related cervical myelopathy when the patient is male, given the female-predominant epidemiology of RA.
